page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Loss of water
lines: On gentle heating it first loses its six
steps.why: The water molecules are held in the crystal lattice only, so they are driven off at a lower temperature than the one that breaks up the nitrate itself. The heating therefore happens in two stages, and the question asks what happens, so both stages belong in the answer.
common_mistakes: Going straight to the oxide. The hydrate loses its water first, and that stage is part of the answer.
Writing the hydrate with the wrong number of waters. The one meant here is the hexahydrate, Mg(NO₃)₂·6H₂O.
steps.memory_tip: Water leaves first, then the nitrate breaks up.
steps.margin_note: Name the hydrate as Mg(NO₃)₂·6H₂O and say the water goes first.

steps.label: Decomposition of the salt
lines: On stronger heating the anhydrous salt
steps.why: A group 2 nitrate decomposes to the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. Counting the atoms: two magnesium, four nitrogen and twelve oxygen on each side, so the equation as written is balanced.
common_mistakes: Writing Mg(NO₂)₂ as the product. Magnesium nitrate gives the oxide MgO, not the nitrite.
Leaving the equation unbalanced. Two formula units of the nitrate are needed before the oxygen atoms match.
steps.memory_tip: Nitrate to oxide, with brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen given off.
steps.margin_note: Write both stages; the balanced equation belongs to the second one.

insider_note: The question asks what happens, so the answer names both stages — the water leaving and then the salt decomposing — and finishes with the balanced equation.
